blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Analogy focuses on relationship-based reasoning to find similarities between pairs.
Classification requires identifying the 'Odd One Out' from a given set of options.
Number Series tests pattern recognition using basic arithmetic and logical progressions.
Mastering basic reasoning concepts builds the foundation for complex competitive exam problem-solving.

Concept:

An analogy tests the ability to identify the relationship between two objects and apply the same relationship to another pair. The relationship can be based on function, category, degree, cause–effect, or part–whole.

Common Types of Analogy in SSC:

1. Object – Function

2. Category – Member

3. Degree / Intensity

4. Cause – Effect

5. Part – Whole

Method to Solve Analogy:

1. Identify the exact relation in the first pair.

2. Apply the same relation to the second pair.

3. Avoid choosing answers based on word similarity alone.

Solved Examples:

Knife : Cut :: Pen : Write

Army : Soldier :: School : Student

Hot : Cold :: Day : Night

items:
Concept:

In classification, four objects are given. Three follow a common rule while one does not. The task is to identify the odd one out.

Basis of Classification in SSC:

• Category

• Function

• Structure

• Property

• Usage
Solved Examples:
Chair, Table, Sofa, Bed → Answer: Bed
Iron, Copper, Gold, Wood → Answer: Wood

Identify the single element that does not belong to the group
Determine the missing or next number following a defined pattern

items:
Concept:

Number series questions test the ability to identify a pattern in numbers. SSC usually asks simple and moderate level series.

Common Patterns in SSC:

• Addition or subtraction

• Multiplication or division

• Simple progression

• Squares or multiples
Analogy questions often test subtle relationships like word meanings, antonyms, cause-effect, or number ratios.
In Classification problems, ensure that three options share a common rule before declaring the fourth as the odd one out.
For Number Series, always check prime numbers, squares/cubes, and alternate differences first.
